positions/trinitarian-union-framework/on: God is first the Father, Son and Spirit in a communion of love; in the incarnation the Son united himself to all humanity, healed and reconciled it in his own person, and by the Spirit draws people to share his relationship with the Father; salvation is union and participation rather than primarily a legal transaction.
positions/trinitarian-union-framework/co: God’s primary identity is the Triune communion of love; law and judgement serve that love.
Sin is primarily alienation, bondage and corruption of relationship, including but not reduced to guilt.
In the incarnation, Christ assumed fallen humanity and included all people in his vicarious life, death and resurrection ("one died for all, therefore all died").
Faith is the Spirit-given response that participates in, rather than completes, what God has done in Christ; in stronger forms (Kruger, du Toit) the gospel announces an inclusion already true of all.
Wrath is the opposition of God’s love to what destroys his children, not a hostility needing to be changed into love.
positions/trinitarian-union-framework/or: Draws on Irenaeus, Athanasius and Eastern theosis and on Calvin’s union with Christ; reshaped by John McLeod Campbell (1856), Karl Barth’s doctrine of election (Church Dogmatics II/2, 1942), T. F. and J. B. Torrance; popularised by C. Baxter Kruger (Perichoresis, from 1997), Francois du Toit’s Mirror Bible and Mirror Word, and global "finished work"/grace-message preaching.
positions/trinitarian-union-framework/pr: Joseph Prince (Singapore, grace message, distinct emphases)
Grace Communion International (adopted Trinitarian theology c.2000s)
positions/trinitarian-union-framework/st: It places the person of Christ and the Trinity, rather than an abstract law, at the centre of the gospel.
It takes seriously the pervasive New Testament language of being "in Christ" and of Christ’s representative humanity.
It grounds assurance in who Christ is for all, freeing preaching from fear and conditionality.
Legal critics: it downplays guilt, wrath and the need for personal faith and repentance, and in stronger forms implies universalism.
Many Reformed scholars argue the Torrances misread federal theology and Calvin, who held union and imputation together.
Orthodox observers note that Western inclusion theologies differ from patristic theosis, which is synergistic and sacramental.
positions/trinitarian-union-framework/re: Most academic representatives (T. F. Torrance, Barth) explicitly refused universalism as a system and insisted on faith as real participation.
They reply that they do not deny judgement or substitution but relocate them within the Son’s filial relation to the Father.
positions/trinitarian-union-framework/co: Shapes Torrance-influenced Scottish and American Reformed theology, Trinitarian ministry networks, and grace-message movements in Africa, Asia and North America.
Has prompted denominational reassessment (e.g. Grace Communion International) and debates about universalism.
positions/theotokos/oneLine: Because the child born of Mary is the eternal Son of God incarnate — one person — Mary is truly the Mother of God, not merely the mother of a human nature.
positions/theotokos/coreClaims/0: Mothers give birth to persons, not natures; the person born of Mary is God the Word.
positions/theotokos/coreClaims/1: The title primarily safeguards the unity of Christ's person (communicatio idiomatum).
positions/theotokos/coreClaims/2: Mary is honoured as the one who gave the eternal Son his human flesh.
positions/theotokos/coreClaims/3: Elizabeth already calls her ‘the mother of my Lord’ (Luke 1:43).
positions/theotokos/origin: Used in Alexandria in the 3rd–4th centuries (Origen per Socrates, Alexander of Alexandria, Athanasius); in the prayer Sub tuum praesidium (papyrus perhaps 3rd–4th century); defended by Cyril of Alexandria and affirmed at Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451).
positions/theotokos/proponentsOther/3: most modern Protestant theologians (as a Christological title)
positions/theotokos/strongestArguments/0: It follows necessarily from the one person of Christ: if Jesus is God, his mother is the Mother of God.
positions/theotokos/strongestArguments/1: It protects against dividing Christ into a divine Son and a human son.
positions/theotokos/strongestArguments/2: It is ancient, ecumenical (Ephesus, Chalcedon) and accepted by Luther and Calvin.
positions/theotokos/strongestObjections/: It may suggest that Mary is the source of the divine nature or a goddess-mother.
The Church of the East prefers ‘Mother of Christ’ to protect divine impassibility.
Some Protestants avoid it because it can fuel excessive Marian devotion.
positions/theotokos/responses/0: Every defender clarifies that Mary is mother of the Word according to the flesh, not of the divine nature.
positions/theotokos/responses/1: The 1994 Catholic–Assyrian declaration accepted both ‘Mother of God’ and ‘Mother of Christ our God and Saviour’ as legitimate expressions.
positions/theotokos/consequences/0: The foundation of all subsequent Marian theology and devotion, including great Marian churches (Santa Maria Maggiore, rebuilt after 431).
positions/theotokos/consequences/1: A Christological touchstone in the Nestorian controversy.
positions/christotokos/oneLine: Mary should be called ‘Mother of Christ’ (Christotokos), since she gave birth to the humanity united to the Word, not to the eternal Godhead.
positions/christotokos/coreClaims/0: The Godhead has no mother; the eternal Word was not born in time.
positions/christotokos/coreClaims/1: ‘Theotokos’ risks implying that Mary is the source of divinity or that the divine nature suffered and changed.
positions/christotokos/coreClaims/2: ‘Christotokos’ names the one Christ in whom Godhead and manhood are united.
positions/christotokos/coreClaims/3: The Church of the East honours Mary highly as ‘Mother of Christ our God and Saviour’.
positions/christotokos/keyTexts/2: Hebrews 7:3 (Melchizedek ‘without mother’, applied to Christ's divinity)
positions/christotokos/origin: Proposed by Nestorius as a compromise between Theotokos and Anthropotokos (428); condemned at Ephesus (431); maintained in East Syriac liturgy.
positions/christotokos/proponentsOther/1: Church of the East liturgical tradition
positions/christotokos/strongestArgument: It is biblical language; Scripture never says ‘Mother of God’ explicitly.
It guards against pagan mother-goddess associations.
It protects divine impassibility and immutability.
positions/christotokos/strongestObjectio: It implies that the one born of Mary is someone other than God the Word.
Elizabeth calls her ‘mother of my Lord’ (Luke 1:43), and ‘Lord’ is the divine name.
It undermines the single subject of Christ's saving acts.
positions/christotokos/responses/0: East Syriac theologians insist that Christ is one, so ‘Mother of Christ’ includes his divinity without confusing the natures.
positions/christotokos/consequences/0: Precipitated the Council of Ephesus and the separation of the Church of the East.
positions/christotokos/consequences/1: Recognised as orthodox in intent in the 1994 Catholic–Assyrian declaration.
positions/perpetual-virginity/altNames/1: Virginity before, during and after birth
positions/perpetual-virginity/oneLine: Mary remained a virgin before, during and after the birth of Jesus; the ‘brothers and sisters’ of Jesus are relatives — Joseph's children by a previous marriage (Eastern view) or cousins (Jerome's view).
positions/perpetual-virginity/coreClaims: Mary conceived virginally by the Holy Spirit (shared by nearly all Christians).
She remained a virgin throughout her life, wholly dedicated to God.
Greek adelphos and Hebrew/Aramaic usage can denote kin more broadly.
Jesus entrusting Mary to John (John 19:26–27) implies she had no other sons to care for her.
positions/perpetual-virginity/origin: The Protoevangelium of James (c. 150) presents Joseph as an elderly widower; defended by Origen, Athanasius, Epiphanius, Jerome (Against Helvidius, 383), Ambrose and Augustine; the title ‘ever-virgin’ appears at Constantinople II (553) and the Lateran Synod (649).
positions/perpetual-virginity/proponents: John Wesley (affirmed in his Letter to a Roman Catholic, 1749)
positions/perpetual-virginity/strongestA: It was the near-universal belief of the church from the 4th century, including the major Reformers.
Jesus' entrusting of Mary to John is difficult to explain if she had other sons.
Jesus' ‘brothers’ are never called sons of Mary; James and Joses' mother appears to be another Mary (Mark 15:40).
positions/perpetual-virginity/strongestO: Matthew 1:25 (‘knew her not till she had brought forth’) naturally implies normal marriage afterwards.
The plain meaning of ‘brothers’ and ‘sisters’ (Mark 6:3) is siblings.
The doctrine may reflect later ascetic devaluation of marriage and sexuality.
positions/perpetual-virginity/responses/: Defenders argue that ‘till’ (heos) does not imply a change afterwards (cf. 2 Samuel 6:23; Matthew 28:20).
Hegesippus (2nd century) describes James and Simeon as relatives of Jesus through Clopas, Joseph's brother.
positions/perpetual-virginity/consequenc: Strengthened the ideal of consecrated virginity in early monasticism.
Protestant belief shifted from acceptance (16th century) to widespread rejection (from the 18th–19th centuries).
positions/helvidian-view/name: Helvidian view: Mary had other children
positions/helvidian-view/altNames/0: Antidicomarianites (Epiphanius' label for its ancient holders)
positions/helvidian-view/oneLine: Mary was a virgin when she conceived Jesus but afterwards lived a normal married life with Joseph and bore other children — James, Joses, Judas, Simon and daughters.
positions/helvidian-view/coreClaims/0: Matthew 1:25 implies normal marital relations after Jesus' birth.
positions/helvidian-view/coreClaims/1: The Gospels name Jesus' brothers and mention sisters with Mary (Mark 6:3; Matthew 12:46).
positions/helvidian-view/coreClaims/2: Marriage and motherhood are as honourable as virginity.
positions/helvidian-view/origin: Tertullian appears to have assumed it (On the Flesh of Christ 23; Against Marcion 4.19); argued explicitly by Helvidius at Rome (c. 380), answered by Jerome (383); Bonosus and Jovinian held related views; widespread in modern Protestantism and among many historical-critical scholars.
positions/helvidian-view/proponentsOther: most modern evangelical and Baptist scholars
many critical scholars (e.g. John P. Meier judged it the most probable reading)
positions/helvidian-view/strongestArgume: It takes the most natural meaning of the Gospel texts.
Paul calls James ‘the Lord's brother’ (Galatians 1:19) without qualification.
It honours marriage and family life.
positions/helvidian-view/strongestObject: Against the near-universal patristic and Reformation consensus.
John 19:26–27 is hard to explain if Mary had living sons.
‘Brother’ has a broad range in biblical usage (Genesis 13:8; 14:16).
positions/helvidian-view/responses/0: Holders reply that Jesus' brothers did not yet believe (John 7:5), which explains why Mary was entrusted to John.
positions/helvidian-view/consequences/0: Became the majority Protestant view from the 18th–19th centuries.
positions/helvidian-view/consequences/1: A factor in Protestant–Catholic/Orthodox differences in Marian piety.
positions/immaculate-conception/oneLine: From the first instant of her conception, by a singular grace and in view of the merits of Christ, Mary was preserved free from every stain of original sin.
positions/immaculate-conception/coreClai: Mary was redeemed by Christ — but by preservation rather than by cleansing after the fact.
God fittingly prepared a sinless mother for his Son (‘full of grace’, Luke 1:28).
Mary is the new Eve, created in innocence as Eve was.
The doctrine was defined infallibly by Pius IX (8 December 1854).
positions/immaculate-conception/origin: Feast of the Conception of Mary from the East (7th–8th century), spreading to England (11th century, Eadmer) and opposed by Bernard (1140) and Aquinas; the Franciscan John Duns Scotus provided the theology of preservative redemption (c. 1305); approved as a pious opinion by Sixtus IV (1476–83); defined by Pius IX in Ineffabilis Deus (1854) after consulting bishops worldwide.
positions/immaculate-conception/stronges: It honours Christ as perfect redeemer: preventing sin is a greater redemption than curing it (Scotus).
It was supported by wide popular devotion and by the consensus of Catholic bishops in 1854.
Kecharitomene (Luke 1:28) can be read as a permanent state of grace.
Bernadette's report at Lourdes (1858) of the Lady saying ‘I am the Immaculate Conception’ was received by Catholics as confirmation.
No explicit scriptural basis; Romans 3:23 says ‘all have sinned’.
Major medieval theologians (Bernard, Aquinas, Bonaventure) rejected it.
Orthodox: it presupposes an Augustinian view of inherited guilt they do not share, and it seems to separate Mary from the rest of humanity that Christ came to save.
Protestants and Orthodox reject the authority of the 1854 definition and its unilateral, papal mode.
positions/immaculate-conception/response: Catholic theologians argue that Aquinas' objection (Mary must need redemption) is answered by preservative redemption.
Development of doctrine (Newman) explains how an implicit belief can be defined later.
ARCIC (2005) found the doctrine's content could be consonant with Scripture when understood in light of grace, while the authority question remained.
positions/immaculate-conception/conseque: Major Marian shrines and devotion (Lourdes, Miraculous Medal); the USA's patronal feast.
Precedent for the papal definition of 1870 and of the Assumption (1950).
A further barrier to Catholic–Orthodox and Catholic–Protestant agreement.
